description.narrative: The development objective of the proposed operation is to strengthen the Government's capacity to mobilize resources in the case ofdisaster and to promote risk reduction.

The objective of the Development Policy Loan with a Catastrophe Deferred Drawdown Option Program for Peru is to strengthen the Government's capacity to mobilize resources in the case of disaster and to promote risk reduction. The Government of Peru (GoP) will begin implementing the Strategic Budget Program for Disaster Vulnerability Reduction and Emergency Response (Programa Presupuestal Estrategico de Reduccion de Vulnerabilidad y Atencion de Emergencias por Desastres, PPE-RVAE) under the results-based budgeting framework and will focus primarily on health, water and sanitation as priority sectors. In addition, the formulation of an overall financial strategy, while seeking the right balance of emergency funds, excellent debt management service, and greater market access to additional funding, may be considered one of the key aspects of this operation. Throughout this process, the Ministry of Economy and Finance (MEF) aims to increase its capacity to mobilize resources in the event of a disaster and to strengthen financial and technical mechanisms related to investments in vulnerability reduction. The GoP is implementing a set of activities related to disaster risk management under the framework of a national vulnerability reduction policy. This document describes the actions undertaken to date by the GoP in support of these activities. The Bank agrees that this national policy constitutes a good foundation to further reduce the country's exposure to disaster risk in a sustainable manner.

title.narrative: National Budget includes an annual specific allocation for the Budgetary Program for Disaster Vulnerability Reduction and Emergency Response (PREVAED)

target.value: National Budget includes a specific budget allocation for the PREVAED

comment.narrative:
<p>Original: National Budget (2012 and 2013) includes a specific budget allocation for the PREVAED.</p>

<p>Baseline (2010): No budget allocated</p>

<p>Status (2013): Budget allocations were PEN 54.4 million (2011), PEN 138.9 million (2012), and PEN 708.7 million (2013).</p>

<p>Revised (2013, 2016): National Budget (2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019) includes a specific budget allocation for the PREVAED.</p>

<p>Status (2019): The budget allocations were PEN 820 million (2014), PEN 1,000 million (2015), PEN 2,088 million (2016), PEN 748 million (2017), and PEN 875 million (2018). For 2019, the budget allocation was PEN 1,349 million.</p>

actual.value: The budget allocations were PEN 820 million (2014), PEN 1,000 million (2015), PEN 2,088 million (2016), PEN 748 million (2017), andPEN 875 million (2018). For 2019, the budget allocation was PEN 1,349 million.

title.narrative: At least 30 of the EPS have established contingent funds for disaster risk management in their new pricing structure

comment.narrative:
<p>Original: At least four water and sanitation service companies (EPS) adopted standard technical guidelines to incorporate disaster risk management in their management framework developed by SUNASS. </p>

<p>Baseline (2010): 0 EPS</p>

<p>Status (2013): 5 EPS integrated DRM in their management frameworks. </p>

<p>Revised (2013): Same expected target continued, and the National Water and Sanitation Plan 2014–2021 includes disaster risk management considerations. </p>

<p>Status (2016): 23 EPS have established contingent funds for DRM. The National Sanitation Plan 2014–2021 was being updated to incorporate the policies of the new government and approval was expected in the next few months. </p>

<p>Revised (2016): At least 30 EPS have established contingent funds for disaster risk management in their new pricing structure.</p>

<p>Baseline (2016): 23/50 EPS</p>

<p>Status (2019): 41 EPS have established contingent funds for DRM. The tariff studies which include these contingent funds are valid for five years, and on average 2% of the annual income of the EPS is allocated for DRM activities. The Water and Sanitation National Plan 2017–2021 (approved DS N° 018-2017-VIVIENDA) includes policy guidelines and indicators to measure actions related to mitigating climate change and disaster risks in water and sanitation services. </p>

title.narrative: Risk Analysis is included in all Public Investment Projects (PIPs) for new hospitals

target.value: All PIPs for new hospitals built after 2011 include risk analysis during the formulation phase

comment.narrative:
<p>Original and Renewals: All PIPs for new hospitals built after 2011 include risk analysis during the formulation phase</p>

<p>Baseline (2010): Not accounted in 2010</p>

<p>Status (2013): The sector has guidelines for the incorporation of risk analysis into new infrastructure projects. No new hospital projects reported.</p>

<p>Revised (2013, 2016): Same expected target continued.</p>

<p>Status (2019): The National Safer Hospitals Policy was updated in 2017 and adopted by Supreme Decree and mandates all health facilities to integrate risk reduction. To ensure implementation of the policy in 2018 a multi-sectorial commission on safer hospitals was created by Ministerial Decree. In April 2019, it was announced by MINSA that 48 new health infrastructures would be built.</p>

actual.value: The National Safer Hospitals Policy was updated in 2017 and adopted by Supreme Decree and mandates all health facilities to integrate risk reduction. To ensure implementation of the policy in 2018 a multi-sectorial commission on safer hospitals was created by Ministerial Decree. In April 2019, it was announced by MINSA that 48 new health infrastructures would be built.

title.narrative: Update the guidelines to include disaster risk management policies in public investment

baseline.value: The National Public Investment System (SNIP) 2008 includes emergency projects

target.value: Update the guidelines to include disaster risk management policies in public investment

comment.narrative:
<p>Original: MEF revised its current framework for implementation of post-disaster public investments. </p>

<p>Baseline: SNIP2008 for emergency project.</p>

<p>Status (2013): MEF issued guidelines for reconstruction project profiles under the SNIP framework (Annex 17 - Directorate Resolution 008-2012-EF/63.01).</p>

<p>Revised (2013): MEF issued sector guidelines for post-disaster rehabilitation for infrastructure in water and sanitation, health, education sectors.</p>

<p>Status (2016): MEF issued guidelines for post-disaster rehabilitation for infrastructure in water and sanitation but decided not to issue specific guidelines for other sectors.</p>

<p>Revised (2016): Update the guidelines to include disaster risk management policies in public investment.</p>

<p>Status (2019): In 2017, a new public investment system was approved (Invierte.pe), which required an update to all processes. The general guide to formulate and evaluate PIPs was approved in September 2019 and includes guidelines to integrate DRM considerations in the PIP formulation cycle. (MEF Directoral Resolution Nº 004-2019-EF/63.01)</p>

title.narrative: MEF continues to implement the Financial Protection Strategy against disasters mobilizing new financial instruments to reduce the fiscal impact of disasters, including insurance for public assets and

target.value: MEF continues to implement the Financial Protection Strategy against disasters mobilizing new financial instruments

comment.narrative:
<p>Original: MEF mobilized a pool of financial instruments to better respond to and reduce the financial impacts of disasters. </p>

<p>Baseline (2010): None</p>

<p>Status (2013): The Directorate for Disaster Risk Management was created under MEF and contingent lines of credit were under preparation: CAF US$300 million, Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) US$300 million, and Inter-American Development Bank (IADB) US$300 million.</p>

<p>Revised (2013): MEF has issued the Risk Financing Strategy to be submitted to the PCM under the SINAGERD Framework. </p>

<p>Status (2016): MEF’s risk committee approved the Risk Financing Strategy, known as the ‘Financial Protection Strategy against Disasters’ and presented it to the PCM in 2016.
 < br />
Revised (2016): MEF continues to implement the Financial Protection Strategy against disasters, by mobilizing new financial instruments to reduce the fiscal impact of disasters, including insurance for public assets and risk transfer instruments.</p>

<p>Baseline (2016): 0 instruments</p>

<p>Status (2019): MEF has mobilized a new risk transfer instrument. In February 2018, Peru joined Chile, Colombia, and Mexico as part of the Pacific Alliance for a catastrophe bond issued by the World Bank (US$1.36 billion), in which Peru has US$200 million in risk insurance for earthquake risks for three years. Peru received a US$60 million payout after the 2019 earthquake (8 Mw), which was channeled to FONDES. Efforts are under way to develop a risk transfer instrument for hydrometeorological hazards.</p>

actual.value: MEF has mobilized a new risk transfer instrument. In February 2018, Peru joined Chile, Colombia, and Mexico as part of the Pacific Alliance for a catastrophe bond issued by the World Bank (US$1.36 billion), in which Peru has US$200 million in risk insurance for earthquake risks for three years. Peru received a US$60 million payout after the 2019 earthquake (8 Mw), which was channeled to FONDES. Efforts are under way to develop a risk transfer instrument for hydrometeorological hazards.

title.narrative: Retrofitting works have initiated in at least five hospitals which have finalized structural vulnerability studies

baseline.value: 1 study of structural vulnerability in hospitals in 2010

target.value: Retrofitting works have initiated in at least five hospitals which have finalized structural vulnerability studies

comment.narrative:
<p>Original: At least 20% completion of studies of structural vulnerability of MINSA hospitals that qualify for retrofitting</p>

<p>Baseline (2010): One study of structural vulnerability in hospitals in 2010</p>

<p>Status (2013): 14 structural vulnerability studies initiated; this is 30% of MINSA hospitals that qualify for retrofitting.</p>

<p>Revised (2013, 2016): Retrofitting works have been initiated in at least five hospitals which have finalized structural vulnerability studies.</p>

<p>Status (2019): 15 structural vulnerability studies were completed by 2016. In 2017, MINSA signed an agreement with the Peruvian-Japanese Center for Seismic Research and Disaster Mitigation (Centro Peruano Japonés de Investigaciones Sísmicas y Mitigación de Desastres, CISMID) of the National Engineering University to elaborate technical files for retrofitting works in five hospitals in Lima. In early2020, the five technical files with final engineering designs were completed by CISMID for the retrofitting works in these hospitals. The five hospitals are included in the public investment system and have been allocated an estimated US$24 million; works are expected to be completed only by March 2022 due to the delays in initiating the works due to the pandemic.</p>

actual.value: 15 structural vulnerability studies completed and in 2017 MINSA signed an agreement with CISMID to elaborate technical files for retrofitting works in 5 hospitals in Lima. No retrofitting works have started.
